content:
Apple has submitted its proposal to the court regarding the fees it would charge for transactions conducted outside the App Store in the Epic Games case. Details below.

Apple Files Proposal for App Store External Transaction Commissions

After multiple attempts to halt proceedings in the district court to determine what fees, if any, Apple may charge for transactions conducted outside of its App Store IAP system, Apple has now submitted its proposal outlining its proposed fee structure.

Apple's submission comes as the Supreme Court denied Apple's request to halt lower court proceedings. Apple is awaiting Supreme Court review of a ruling finding it in potential contempt for charging a 27% commission on App Store external transactions, in alleged violation of an injunction. Previously, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers issued an injunction requiring Apple to allow developers to steer users to alternative purchasing methods.

Apple had argued in the lower court, and subsequently in the Supreme Court, that the Court's ruling could affect the outcome of the fee determination proceedings, and that such proceedings should therefore be paused until the Court issues its ruling. However, the Supreme Court denied Apple's request, allowing the lower court proceedings to continue during the review.

Accordingly, Apple has now submitted its proposal, which is as follows:

Standard apps (subject to the 30% In-App Purchase ("IAP") commission) would be 15%; the Video Partner Program ("VPP"), News Partner Program ("NPP"), and Mini Apps Partner Program ("MPP"), as well as subscription renewals, would be 10%; apps under the Small Business Programme would be 5%.

Apple said that "factual and expert evidence regarding these proposed commission rates has also been submitted alongside." The company added:

Apple added that its "proposed external link commissions are also comparable to commissions charged by competing App Store marketplaces," including Google Play, the Samsung Galaxy Store, and Amazon's Android App Marketplace.

The company also noted that "Google Play Store's standard rate for external links is 20%—a 'standard' rate, 15% programme rate, and 10% subscription rate—rates to which Epic has also agreed."

Apple stated that it continues to believe that the fee determination proceedings should be halted while the case is before the Supreme Court, and noted that this submission is made solely to comply with Judge Gonzalez Rogers's instructions.

The company also pointed out that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the district court's blanket prohibition on charging commissions on external link transactions, and noted that such commissions are only problematic if they are effectively anticompetitive.

Following the submission of the proposal, Epic will have the opportunity to respond, and Apple anticipates filing its brief in the Supreme Court case by September 14.

You can read Apple's full remand proposal below.
